267.title: Where have you hidden (Spiritual Canticle)
267.hook: the soul searches the woods and fields asking where the beloved went
267.howItsDone: Carmelites and many Catholics pray with John's Spiritual Canticle and his commentary on it, and the Church reads the Song of Songs as a love song between God and the soul, and between Christ and the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dark cloud, a cloud that lights the night. Your line was walk by faith. Today, the love poem John began in his prison cell.

You wake up, and the other side of the bed is empty. Still warm. They were just here. You call their name. Nothing. You check the kitchen, the porch, the yard. You start asking anyone you see: have you seen them? Which way did they go? That's how John of the Cross opens his longest poem, the Spiritual Canticle. Not with an answer. With a question, half a cry, from someone who was loved and then found herself alone.
screen: `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE BED.` → `STILL WARM.` → `HAVE YOU SEEN THEM?`

segments.voice: First, the cry. The poem's first line, in John's Spanish: "¿Adónde te escondiste, Amado, y me dejaste con gemido?" Where have you hidden, Beloved, and left me moaning? The bride is the soul. The Beloved is God, and for John, Christ. He's modeling it on the Song of Songs, where the bride says, in the Douay-Rheims: "In my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, and found him not." Second, the search. The bride doesn't sit and wait. She goes out. She asks the shepherds on the hills. She crosses mountains and riverbanks. Then she turns to the woods and thickets themselves, planted by the Beloved's hand: has he passed by here? Third, the answer. And creation answers her. In John's Spanish, the woods say he passed through these groves in haste, pouring out a thousand graces, and just by looking at them as he went, "vestidos los dejó de hermosura," he left them clothed in beauty. The world is lovely, the poem says, because God glanced at it on his way through. Fourth, not enough. Here's the ache. The bride isn't satisfied with the trees. They're beautiful, but they're traces, messengers. She wants him. John says this is what happens as love grows: the world's beauty points to God, and makes you want God more, not less. Nature isn't a substitute; it's a trail of footprints. And the poem keeps going, for dozens of stanzas, until the bride finds the Beloved.
screen: `WHERE HAVE YOU HIDDEN, BELOVED?` · `SHE ASKS THE WOODS AND HILLS.` · `HE LEFT THEM CLOTHED IN BEAUTY.` · `FOOTPRINTS, NOT THE BELOVED.` · then, large: `¿ADÓNDE TE ESCONDISTE, AMADO?`

segments.voice: If you can, step outside or to a window and find one living thing: a tree, a patch of sky, a weed in a crack, a bird. Look at it slowly, as if someone you love had just walked past it. If you pray, ask it John's question, where have you hidden, and listen; if you don't, let its beauty be a trace of something larger.

268.title: The log in the fire (Dark Night 2.10)
268.hook: wet wood hisses and blackens before it becomes flame
268.howItsDone: Catholic spiritual directors use John's image of the log in the fire to reassure people who feel more aware of their faults as they grow in prayer, and his Living Flame of Love is read as the fulfillment of that image.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Spiritual Canticle: Beloved, and woods clothed in beauty. Your line was clothed in beauty. Today, a picture of the night from a fireplace.

Put a damp log on a campfire and wait for a big, cheerful flame. Instead you get hissing. Popping. Water bubbling out of the ends of the log. Gray smoke in your eyes. The bark goes black and ugly. It smells bad. It looks like the fire is ruining the wood, and you start to wonder if it'll ever catch. Then, slowly, it does. John of the Cross uses exactly that kind of fire.
screen: `A CAMPFIRE WITH DAMP WOOD.` → `HISSING, SMOKE, BLACKENED BARK.` → `THEN, SLOWLY, IT CATCHES.`

segments.voice: First, the stages. In the Dark Night, book two, chapter ten, John walks through it. When fire first touches a log, it doesn't set it ablaze. It dries it, driving out the dampness, so the wood seems to weep. Then it blackens it, makes it dark and ugly, even gives off a bad smell. Only as it dries does the fire give it heat and light. At the end, the wood becomes fire itself, as bright and hot as the flame. Second, the log is the soul. The fire is God's love. When that love first gets close, John says, the soul doesn't feel lit up. It feels worse. It suddenly sees its own damp and dark places, faults it didn't know it had. Third, the surprise. Here's John's key point. The fire isn't making the wood ugly. The ugliness was already in the wood. The fire is drawing it out, so it can be burned away. So when someone who's trying to love God suddenly feels more aware of their failings, John says, that's often not a sign of getting worse. It's the smoke. The fire is working. Fourth, the flame. The same fire that hurt at first becomes the one that delights. The log doesn't stay a log with a fire next to it. It becomes flame. John wrote a whole other poem about that end, the Living Flame of Love. For John, the smoke is part of the burning.

segments.voice: Think of one fault you've been noticing in yourself lately, maybe more than before: impatience, envy, a sharp tongue. Instead of beating yourself up, picture it as smoke rising off a log, damp coming out so it can burn clean. If you pray, let God's love keep working on it; if you don't, be gentle with yourself, the way you'd wait out a smoky fire.

269.title: In the evening, love (Sayings of Light and Love)
269.hook: at the end we will be judged on love
269.howItsDone: Catholics often quote John's saying on the evening of life, which the Catechism cites in its teaching on judgment, and many make an evening examen asking how they loved that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Living Flame: first it hisses and blackens, then it becomes flame. Your line was first smoke, then flame. Today, one sentence John left behind.

A final exam with a whole life on it. What would the questions be? The easy guess is a report card. How much got done. How much got earned. Were the rules kept. How many people know the name. Maybe a section on religion: enough prayers, enough Sundays, the right beliefs. John of the Cross wrote down what he thought would be on that exam. It's one line, from a small collection of his sayings, short enough to fit on your palm. Today's word is how it begins.
screen: `THE FINAL EXAM OF YOUR LIFE.` → `A REPORT CARD?` → `ONE LINE ON A PALM.`

segments.voice: First, the sayings. Tradition says John wrote short, sharp sayings on slips of paper for the friars and nuns he guided. They were gathered later as the Sayings of Light and Love. Some are a single sentence. Second, the line. In John's Spanish: "A la tarde te examinarán en el amor." In the evening, you will be examined in love. The evening is the end of life. The exam has one subject. Not how much you knew about prayer, or how many dark nights you understood. Love. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes this line when it teaches about judgment. Third, where he got it. It's not John's invention. It comes straight from Jesus's picture of the last judgment in Matthew's Gospel, where the nations are sorted by whether they fed the hungry, welcomed the stranger, visited the sick and the prisoner. The king says, in the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." John knew this passage from both sides: the boy washing the sick in the hospital, the prisoner in the dark room. Fourth, what to do about it. Near the end of his life, John wrote to a Carmelite nun who was upset at how his superiors were treating him. He told her not to grieve over it, and added: where there is no love, put love, and you will draw out love. Not wait for it. Put it there. The nights, the fire, the nada all come back to this. The whole point was love.
screen: `SAYINGS ON SLIPS OF PAPER.` · `EXAMINED IN LOVE.` · `THE LEAST OF THESE.` · `WHERE THERE IS NO LOVE, PUT LOVE.` · then, large: `A LA TARDE TE EXAMINARÁN EN EL AMOR.`

segments.voice: Picture this evening, the end of today, and look back on it: what would love have done? Let one face come to mind, someone hungry, lonely, sick, difficult, or simply waiting to hear from you, and ask what one thing love needs you to do for them. If you pray, ask God to show you; if you don't, trust the first honest answer.

270.title: Úbeda, 1591
270.hook: dying, he asked to hear the Song of Songs, not the prayers for the dying
270.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint John of the Cross on December 14, the day he died in Úbeda, and the Church's prayers for the dying are still read at deathbeds, sometimes alongside readings a person has asked for.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tarde: in the evening of life, you'll be examined in love. Your line was judged on love. Today, John's own evening comes.

By 1591, John of the Cross has lost almost everything the world counts. The leaders of the reform he helped start have turned against him in a quarrel over how it should be run. He's stripped of every office and sent to a remote friary in the south. Then he gets sick: a fever, and an infection in his leg that won't heal. He needs a town with doctors. The story goes that he could have gone to a friary where he was loved, and chose Úbeda, where he wasn't known. The prior there doesn't like him.
screen: `STRIPPED OF EVERY OFFICE.` → `A FEVER, AN INFECTED LEG.` → `A PRIOR WHO DOESN'T LIKE HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the prior. The man in charge at Úbeda resented John and for weeks treated him coldly, complaining about the cost of his care and giving him one of the poorest cells. John didn't fight back. The story told about the prior is that he later wept and changed his mind about John. Second, the sores. The infection spread. The doctors cut into his leg again and again, without anything like a modern painkiller. The friars who nursed him remembered that he hardly complained, and thanked everyone who helped him. Third, the last night. On December 13, he kept asking what time it was. When they told him it was almost midnight, the story goes, he said he would soon go to sing the morning prayers in heaven. The friars began to read the Church's prayers for the dying. John stopped them, gently, and asked instead for the Song of Songs, the love poetry of the Bible. They read it to him, and he said: what precious pearls. Fourth, the song. The accounts don't say exactly which lines. Here are some from that book, in the Douay-Rheims: "Arise, make haste, my love, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For winter is now past, the rain is over and gone." A man who'd written so much about dark nights, dying in a cold cell, asking to hear about spring. He died just after midnight, on December 14, 1591. The Church keeps his feast on that day. For him, it seems, death wasn't a final night. It was the Beloved saying: arise, and come.

segments.voice: Find Song of Songs 2:10 to 13 if you have a Bible nearby, or simply recall those lines about winter being past. Think of a winter in your own life that's ending, or that you hope will end. If you pray, hear the words as God's to you; if you don't, let them be about spring.

271.title: A doctor for the dark
271.hook: named a Doctor of the Church in 1926; a guide for anyone in the night
271.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of St. John of the Cross on December 14, and spiritual directors often point people in long seasons of dryness to his Dark Night and Ascent of Mount Carmel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Úbeda, 1591. Dying, John asked to hear the Song of Songs, not the prayers for the dying. Your line was arise and come. Today, the last of eighteen days with little Seneca.

A long, dark stretch can take many shapes. A diagnosis. A grief that won't lift. A prayer life gone flat and silent for months. Some people in that place say the same thing: I thought I was doing it wrong. A small friar, jailed by his own brothers, wrote about that stretch in poems and commentaries. More than three centuries after he died, the Church gave him a title it gives to teachers it holds up for everyone. Today: a doctor for the dark.
screen: `A LONG, DARK STRETCH.` → `I THOUGHT I WAS DOING IT WRONG.` → `A DOCTOR FOR THE DARK.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Doctor comes from the Latin docere, to teach. A Doctor of the Church isn't a physician. It's a teacher the whole Church is told it can trust. The title asks for three things: a holy life, deep learning, and a pope's declaration. It's rare. The first four were named in 1298: Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome and Gregory the Great. Second, the long road. John died in 1591, mistrusted by some of his own superiors. He was canonized a saint in 1726, and in 1926 Pope Pius XI named him a Doctor of the Church. He's known as the Mystical Doctor. Third, what he teaches. Look back over these weeks. The dark night: when prayer goes dry, God may not be gone. Dry is not gone. The three signs: the longing stays. Nada: nothing, then everything. Remora. The log that smokes before it catches. Together, it fits in one surprising sentence: the dark can be part of the road, not the end of it. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary Tuesday. John is careful. In the Dark Night he says some dryness comes from melancholy or bad health, and that isn't the night he means. He never makes pain holy for its own sake. What he gives people in the dark is company, and a map. Someone has been here and wrote down the way through. A psalm says it to God, in the Douay-Rheims: "night shall be light as the day." The Mystical Doctor spent his life on that line.
screen: `DOCERE — TO TEACH.` · `CANONIZED 1726, DOCTOR 1926.` · `THE DARK CAN BE PART OF THE ROAD.` · `COMPANY, AND A MAP.` · then, large: `NIGHT SHALL BE LIGHT AS THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person in a dark stretch right now, and don't try to fix it; just hold their face for a moment. Ask whether it would help them to know someone has walked this road before, maybe through one line from these weeks: dry is not gone. Only if it feels kind, not like a lecture. If you pray, hold them in the quiet.

272.title: A restless young man (1915)
272.hook: born in France, orphaned young, drifting through Cambridge and Columbia
272.howItsDone: Many Catholics read Thomas Merton's autobiography as a modern story of conversion, and Augustine's line about the restless heart is often quoted in Catholic preaching and in the Catechism itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mystical Doctor: John of the Cross, a guide for the dark. Your line was the night is a way. Today, a new guide, and a very different life.

Rome, 1933. An eighteen-year-old wanders the city on his own. Both his parents are dead. He has money from a guardian, a head full of novels, and no plan. He goes into the old churches, not to pray, but to look at the mosaics, because he likes art. Standing in front of those gold and blue walls, something catches in him that he can't name. He'll spend years running from it. His name is Thomas Merton. He'll become the most famous monk in America, and for the next eighteen days he's the guide. Today: a restless young man.
screen: `ROME, 1933. EIGHTEEN, AND ALONE.` → `INTO THE CHURCHES FOR THE ART.` → `A RESTLESS YOUNG MAN.`

segments.voice: First, the losses. Merton was born on January 31, 1915, in Prades, a small town in the south of France. His father was a painter from New Zealand, his mother an American artist. When he was six, his mother died of cancer. When he was fifteen, his father died too. Then he was moved around: schools in France and England, holidays with relatives, a guardian in London. A boy with a suitcase, never quite at home. Second, the drifting. At Cambridge he drank, stayed out, failed at being careful, and left after a year he later looked back on with real shame. His guardian sent him to America. At Columbia University in New York he was clever, funny, restless. He wrote for the humor magazine, loved jazz, and flirted with politics. Busy all the time, happy almost never. Third, the mosaics. In those Roman churches he'd looked at pictures of Christ, and for the first time he wanted to know who that was. He didn't act on it yet. He just couldn't forget it. Fourth, why restless is a start. Long before Merton, Augustine wrote at the opening of his Confessions that the human heart is restless until it rests in God. Catholics have loved that sentence for sixteen hundred years. It doesn't treat restlessness as a failure. It treats it as a sign you're made for something you haven't found yet. Merton's early life looks like a mess. Read with Augustine, it looks like a search.

273.howItsDone: Adults who become Catholic today usually walk a path of study and prayer called the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults, and are often baptized or received into the Church at the Easter Vigil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, inquietum: Merton, orphaned, drifting through Cambridge and Columbia. Your line was restless is a start. Today, the restlessness starts to go somewhere.

New York, 1937. Merton is at Columbia, and he buys a book for a class: a history of medieval philosophy. On the train home he opens it and sees the little Latin stamp saying a Catholic censor approved it. He's so annoyed he nearly throws it out the window. He doesn't. He reads it, and one idea in it cracks something open. A year later he's standing in a priest's doorway on a rainy afternoon, saying: I want to become a Catholic.
screen: `A BOOK HE NEARLY THREW OUT.` → `ONE IDEA CRACKS IT OPEN.` → `I WANT TO BECOME A CATHOLIC.`

segments.voice: First, the idea. The book was Étienne Gilson's The Spirit of Medieval Philosophy. Merton had assumed God was a vague, fuzzy feeling. Gilson showed him the medieval idea that God is not one more thing in the universe, but being itself, the reason anything exists at all. Merton later wrote that this gave him a whole new respect for the faith. Second, the friends: a professor named Mark Van Doren, a poet friend named Robert Lax. And a surprise: a Hindu monk visiting New York, called Bramachari, who told him to read Augustine's Confessions and The Imitation of Christ, the great books of his own Western tradition. Third, the church. One Sunday in August 1938 he went, alone, to Mass at Corpus Christi Church near the university. He left before the end, nervous, and walked down the street happier than he'd felt in years. Weeks later, reading about the poet Gerard Manley Hopkins becoming a Catholic, he put the book down, walked through the rain to the rectory, and asked. On November 16, 1938, he was baptized. Fourth, the word. Convert comes from the Latin convertere, to turn around. The Catholic twist: the turning isn't only the person's own work. In John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "No man can come to me, except the Father, who hath sent me, draw him." Looking back, Merton saw it the same way. A book, a teacher, a monk, a Mass. Someone was drawing him the whole time.
